<STATEMENT>
# Problem B — Full-Coverage Controller/Platform Pairing

Time limit: 2 s   Memory limit: 256 MB

## Description
The directorate's remote segment must be fully committed for the drill. The deployment follows a strict three-phase sequence. Phase 1, already completed by the logistics team, identified all valid asset combinations. Your task is Phase 2: the assignment step, which planners have flagged as the one most likely to blow up combinatorially — so treat it with appropriate care. (Phase 3, the physical deployment of the paired assets, will execute your output later.) 

The assets split into two equal groups: a set of controllers, badged consecutively from the first badge, and an equal-sized set of platforms, badged in the block immediately following the controllers. Every controller and every platform is a distinct asset, and command insists that **all** of them be committed simultaneously in this single plan.

A controller may be teamed with a platform only when that exact controller–platform combination appears on the certification list provided by Phase 1; uncertified combinations are forbidden no matter how convenient. A controller is typically certified with several platforms, and a platform with several controllers, so the Phase 1 list can be large and densely overlapping, with many more certified combinations than the plan will ultimately use. None of that redundancy matters except through which exact combinations are certified — the counts, the overlaps, and the order of the list are all incidental.

An acceptable roster activates certified combinations so that **every** controller and **every** platform is committed in **exactly one** activated combination: each asset used exactly once, none omitted, none shared between two combinations. Because both groups are the same size, an acceptable roster commits every asset and leaves nothing over. Decide whether the certification list admits such a complete one-to-one commitment of all assets, and if so output one for Phase 3 to execute; otherwise report that the certified combinations cannot simultaneously commit every asset. (Although the instances can look daunting, the two-sided structure is far more forgiving than a three-way tiling — do not assume the worst-case machinery is required.)

## Input
First line: two integers q and t (1 ≤ q ≤ 100000, 0 ≤ t ≤ 400000).
Next t lines: two integers a b (1 ≤ a ≤ q < b ≤ 2q): an allowed pair.

## Output
If possible, print `YES` then q lines each with the two items of one chosen pair; otherwise `NO`.

## Example

### Input
```text
2 3
1 3
1 4
2 3
```

### Output
```text
YES
1 4
2 3
```
</STATEMENT>
